title: Topological Surface Charge Detection via Terahertz Time-domain Spectroscopy
authors: Tong Shen, Yiyang Xie, Yucheng Dai, Yifan Zhang, Yuanze Li, Xufeng Kou, Tian Liang
abstract: The topological magnetoelectric effect (TME) in three-dimensional topological insulators manifests as a quantized surface charge accumulation proportional to an applied magnetic field. Here we demonstrate an optical method using terahertz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS) to detect surface charge accumulation in a chromium-doped (Bi,Sb)$_2$Te$_3$ thin film under oblique incidence, achieving sub-milliradian Faraday rotation precision. Unlike transport probes that require ultralow longitudinal conductivity, this optical technique is robust against finite $σ_L$, degrading by less than $0.3\%$ even when $σ_L \sim σ_T$. We extract the charge accumulation $η/B_z$ from the measured Faraday rotation and show results at $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ coincide within experimental uncertainty. Extending this to axion insulators, we predict that the TME produces an imaginary Faraday rotation linear in frequency, whose slope directly reflects the single-surface charge density. With improved sample thickness and precision, this optical scheme provides a viable pathway toward direct verification of the TME and four-dimensional quantum Hall effect.
summary: This paper reports on an experimental method utilizing Terahertz Time-domain Spectroscopy to optically detect the topological surface charge accumulation predicted by the Topological Magnetoelectric Effect in topological insulator thin films. By measuring Faraday rotation at oblique incidence, the authors demonstrate a technique robust against material conductivity limitations, providing a direct pathway toward verifying fundamental quantum electrodynamic effects.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop an optical method using THz-TDS to directly detect the quantized surface charge accumulation ($\eta/B_z$) associated with the Topological Magnetoelectric Effect (TME) in 3D topological insulators.
main_result: The technique successfully measures Faraday rotation at oblique incidence, demonstrating robustness against finite longitudinal conductivity and showing consistent results across different incident angles ($45^\circ$ vs $60^\circ$).
method: Terahertz Time-domain Spectroscopy (THz-TDS) is employed to measure the Faraday rotation angle ($	heta_F$) in thin films under oblique incidence, allowing for the extraction of surface charge density.
model_or_system: The study uses chromium-doped $(	ext{Bi},	ext{Sb})_2	ext{Te}_3$ thin films exhibiting topological properties. The physics is governed by the TME, which predicts a quantized surface charge accumulation proportional to an applied magnetic field component ($B_z$).
key_observables: Faraday rotation angle ($	heta_F$), extracted surface charge density ($\eta/B_z$), and the frequency-linear imaginary part of the Faraday rotation for axion insulators.
important_parameters: Oblique incidence angles ($45^\circ, 60^\circ$); low temperatures (e.g., $2	ext{ K}$); comparison between optical vs. transport measurements ($\sigma_L/\sigma_T$).
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on modeling the transmitted electric field using transmission and propagation matrices; for axion insulators, approximations like $\phi \ll 1$ are used.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the THz-TDS setup geometry (oblique incidence), time-domain waveforms showing $E_X$ and $E_Y$, angular dependence of Faraday rotation, and comparisons demonstrating the optical method's robustness against longitudinal conductivity ($\sigma_L$).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the TME in TIs, details the THz-TDS experimental setup for measuring oblique incidence effects, derives the relationship between $	heta_F$ and $\eta/B_z$, presents measurements confirming consistency across angles, and discusses extensions to axion insulators.
why_interesting: While not directly related to standard AMO topics like cold atoms or cavity QED, this work involves probing fundamental quantum electrodynamics effects (magnetoelectric coupling) using advanced optical spectroscopy techniques that share conceptual links with light-matter interaction studies in open systems.
